text: Lynn Conway was born in Mount Vernon, New York, in 1938. She experienced gender dysphoria as a child and underwent a gender transition in the 1960s, after which she restarted her career in stealth mode as a contract programmer. At IBM, she worked on the Advanced Computing Systems (ACS) project, where she invented multiple-issue out-of-order dynamic instruction scheduling. After leaving IBM, she joined Xerox PARC in 1973, where she co-authored *Introduction to VLSI Systems* with Carver Mead. She founded the multiproject wafers (MPW) technology and developed the MOSIS system, which enabled rapid prototyping of chip designs. Her work revolutionized VLSI design and established the foundry model for chip manufacturing. Conway also contributed to the development of the Mead–Conway VLSI design methodology, which became a foundational text in the field. She later joined the University of Michigan, where she specialized in visual communications and control systems. In her later years, she became an advocate for transgender rights, raising awareness and promoting understanding of gender identity. She was recognized with numerous awards, including the Computer Pioneer Award, the IEEE EAB Major Educational Innovation Award, and the National Inventors Hall of Fame induction in 2023. Conway coined the term "Conway effect" to describe the phenomenon where marginalized groups are overlooked in historical accounts of innovation. She died in June 2024 at the age of 86.
